lq.ANSWER:
Q1 — Value of a unit and human values

  DEFINITE — single expected answer 

Model answer:  The value of a unit is its participation in the larger order, and this participation is its role; the context is always the larger order, and the value is definite. For example, the value of wheat with respect to the human being is to provide nutrition to the body, and a kilogram of wheat provides the same nutrition irrespective of time, place or person. Similarly, the role of a piece of chalk is to write on the blackboard in the classroom. Extending this to the human being: my participation in the family defines my value in the family. For order in the family, behaviour with a feeling of respect is valuable; I feel happy when I have a feeling of respect, and the other feels happy when I express respect. Living in accordance with human values with human beings leads to mutual happiness, and with the rest of nature leads to mutual prosperity.

Q2 — The four guidelines for value education

  DEFINITE — single expected answer 

Model answer:  (1) Universal — applicable to all human beings and true at all times and places; not dependent on sect, creed, nationality, race or gender. (2) Rational — amenable to logical reasoning and open to questioning; not based on blind beliefs, dogmas or sermons. (3) Verifiable — the student should be able to verify the values on his or her own right, on the basis of natural acceptance and experiential validation, rather than being asked to believe because it is stated. (4) Leading to Harmony — the values must enable us to live in peace and harmony within ourselves and with others (human beings and the rest of nature), covering all dimensions of being and all levels of living.

Q3 — Values and skills

  DEFINITE — single expected answer 

Model answer:  Understanding what to do relates to values (value education), while learning how to do relates to skills (skill development); doing is the practice, guided by values. The problems around us are more due to a lack of values than a lack of skills, but both are required — values and skills are complementary. As for priority, values (what to do) come first and then skills (how to do), though both are needed. The present state of education has become skill-biased, and there is a need to make appropriate changes so that education helps students understand values and develop holistically.
